title: Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:22–38)
hookLine: two people who waited a long time recognize the baby in the temple

cards: The temple courts are loud. Pilgrims, priests, animals, coins changing hands. Forty days after a birth, the law of Moses asked a mother to come to the temple, and a firstborn son was presented to God.
Mary and Joseph carry the baby up to Jerusalem, with the offering the law allowed for families who couldn't afford a lamb: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.

Nobody is watching a young couple from Galilee with a baby and two birds. Nobody except two people: a widow of great age, and a man who has been waiting a long time. Both of them know what they're looking at.

teach.b: Luke introduces Simeon: "the same man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him." Waiting for the comfort of his people.
Luke says the Spirit had shown him he would not die before he saw the one God promised.

teach.h: NOW LETTEST THOU THY SERVANT DEPART.
teach.b: That day he's led into the temple, takes the baby in his arms, and says: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation."
He calls the child a light for the nations and the glory of Israel.

In Latin those first words are Nunc dimittis, and Simeon's song has been sung at the end of the day for many centuries: at evening prayer by Anglicans, at night prayer by Catholics, at vespers by Orthodox Christians.
Then he turns to Mary with a harder word: a sword will pierce her own soul too.
And then Anna. A prophetess, Luke says, very old, married seven years and then a widow, "which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day."

Luke gives a number, eighty-four, and nobody is sure if it's her age or her years as a widow. She comes up that same hour, gives thanks, and starts telling everyone who is waiting too. Notice who recognizes the child.
Not the powerful. A man who came when the Spirit led him, and a widow who kept showing up.

teach.h: MINE EYES HAVE SEEN THY SALVATION.
teach.b: Luke never gives Simeon's age; painters make him old because he speaks of departing in peace. In Luke's telling, waiting isn't sitting still. It's coming back, day after day, looking.

how: Many churches keep the Presentation of the Lord on February 2, often called Candlemas, when candles are blessed. Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis, is sung or said at the close of the day in Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox prayer.

games.why: he takes the child in his arms and says: now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace. a lifetime of waiting ends in a young couple's arms.

practice: Think of someone older who has waited a long time for something, a letter, a recovery, a call from a child: what did the waiting cost them, and what did it teach them?
If you pray, hold them before God; if you don't, honor them quietly in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Nunc dimittis. Latin for now you let go: the first words of Simeon's song, after he held the infant Jesus.

orig.note: Greek: waiting for, ready to welcome. Luke's word for Simeon, and for the people Anna spoke to.

carryVoice: Your line: waiting is not wasted. Next, stargazers from the east, and the road toward Galilee.
